instructions:
You translate one page of Alexander Grothendieck's handwritten mathematical notes (Montpellier archive) from French
into English. The page is a LaTeX transcription of the manuscript. Some passages are already in English (Grothendieck
wrote parts of these notes in English); keep those exactly as they are.

Write the English version of the whole page, as a faithful raw translation for mathematicians: close to the
wording, keeping Grothendieck's abbreviations, telegraphic style, question marks and hesitations. Do not smooth,
complete, correct or explain anything.

Keep every piece of LaTeX exactly as it is:
- every macro and its arguments' structure: \scanpage{...}, \mspage{...}, \margin{...}, \deleted{...},
  \inserted{...}, \unsure{...}, \illegible{...}, \uline{...}, \diagram{...}, environments, line breaks of displays;
- every formula, symbol and diagram: change no mathematics at all, not even an obvious slip;
- \scanpage and \mspage lines unchanged, in their places.
Translate the French words inside \deleted, \inserted, \margin and \unsure too. An \unsure{a|b} with alternative
readings: translate each alternative and keep the | between them (if two French alternatives give the same English,
still keep both). French words inside \text{...} or \mathrm{...} in formulas: translate them only when they are
ordinary words (e.g. \text{si} -> \text{if}); keep names of objects and notation as they are.
Mathematical terms: use the standard English terms (champ -> stack, catégorie fibrée -> fibred category,
topos, site, faisceau -> sheaf, gerbe -> gerbe, fibration, cofibration, équivalence faible -> weak equivalence,
modèle fermé -> closed model, etc.).

Answer in exactly this form, with nothing before the first marker:
=====BEGIN TARGET_NEW=====
(the complete English page)
=====END TARGET_NEW=====
=====NOTES=====
(readings you were unsure how to translate, with the French; or "none")

Shelfmark 103, scan 3.

\scanpage{3}\mspage{2}

taking for $A$ the ``stack'' on $X$ formed of right $F$-torsors, the (Gr)- category of au\deleted{\unsure{ot|tt}}to-equivalences of $A$ with itself is interpreted as the category of ``b\deleted{\unsure{t|l}}itorsors'' under $F$, i.e. of sheaves \inserted{$P$} on which $F$ acts both on the right and on the left, these operations commuting and each of them making $P$ a torsor (on the right or on the left) under $F$, - the composition $\otimes$ being the evident\deleted{\unsure{s|e}} Baer composition. When $F$ is again of the form $\underline{O}_{X}^{*}$ ($\underline{O}_{X}$ being a\unsure{'|.} sheaf of rings, which is no longer assumed necessarily commutative) these bitorsors are also interpreted in terms of \handwritten{``}invertible\handwritten{''} bi-Modules over $\underline{O}_{X}$.

\uline{Structure}. \deleted{\rlap{xxx}\unsure{The|the}} Let $C$ be a (Gr)-category, we associate to it

a) the group $\handwritten{\pi}_{0}(C)$ of isomorphism classes of objects of $C$,

b) the group $\handwritten{\pi}_{1}(C)$ of automorphisms of $1_C$ (unit object of $C$)

c) an action of $\handwritten{\pi}_{0}(C)$ on $\handwritten{\pi}_{1}(C)$, by associating to every object $X$ of $C$ the automorphism \deleted{\rlap{xxxx}\unsure{of 1}} $\handwritten{\rho}(X)$ of $1_C$ deduced from the two isomorphisms
\diagram{\begin{tikzcd}[ampersand replacement=\&]
\mathrm{Aut}(1_C) \handwritten{\arrow[r,shift left=.55ex]\arrow[r,shift right=.55ex]} \& \mathrm{Aut}(X)
\end{tikzcd}}
given by $u\handwritten{\mapsto}u\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X}$ and $u\handwritten{\mapsto}\mathrm{id}_{X}\otimes u$. One proves that $\handwritten{\pi}_{1}(C)$ is a \uline{commutative} group and that one indeed obtains by c) a $\handwritten{\pi}_{0}(C)$-module structure on the latter. This being so, if one chooses for every $a\handwritten{\in}\handwritten{\pi}_{0}(C)$ a representative $L_{a}\handwritten{\in}\mathrm{Ob}\ C$ of $a$, and for two \deleted{\rlap{xxxxxx}objects} $a,b$ an isomorphism
\[
\handwritten{\phi}_{a,b}: L_a\otimes L_b\handwritten{\simeq}L_{ab}\ , 
\]
then for three elements $a,b,c\handwritten{\in}\handwritten{\pi}_{0}(C)$, the associativity isomorphism
\[
(L_a\otimes L_b)\otimes L_c\handwritten{\simeq}L_a\otimes(L_b\otimes L_c)\ ,
\]
taking into account the isomorphisms $\handwritten{\phi}_{a,b}$, $\handwritten{\phi}_{ab,c}$, $\handwritten{\phi}_{b,c}$ and $\handwritten{\phi}_{a,bc}$, can be interpreted as an isomorphism
\[
L_{abc}\handwritten{\simeq}L_{abc}\ ,
\]
or again as tensoring \deleted{\unsure{on|on}}on the left with a well-determined element
\[
f(a,b,c)\handwritten{\in}\handwritten{\pi}_{1}(C)\deleted{\rlap{$\mathrm{xxxxxxxxx}_{\mathrm{xxxxxx}}$}\unsure{1_{C}\quad 1_{C}}}\ .
\]
The $\handwritten{\phi}_{a,b}$ having been chosen, one thus sees that the datum of a functorial associativity isomorphism $(L\otimes L')\otimes L''\handwritten{\simeq}L\otimes(L'\otimes L'')$ is equivalent to the datum of the map
\[
f:\handwritten{\pi}_{0}\mathbin{\mathrm{x}}\handwritten{\pi}_{0}\mathbin{\mathrm{x}}\handwritten{\pi}_{0}\handwritten{\longrightarrow}\handwritten{\pi}_{1}\ .
\]
One then verifies that the standard axiom \deleted{\handwritten{\unsure{(of the pen}}} of self-compatibility of an associativity datum \inserted{\handwritten{(pentagon axiom)}} is expressed precisely by the condition that $f$ be a \handwritten{3}-\uline{cocycle} of the group $\handwritten{\pi}_{\deleted{1}0}$ with values in the group $\handwritten{\pi}_{1}$. On the other hand, the indeterminacy in the choice of the system of isomorphisms $\handwritten{\phi}_{a,b}$ is precisely given by an arbitrary 2-cochain, and one sees that if one changes $\handwritten{\phi}$ by a 2-coc\deleted{\unsure{a}}hain $g$, $f$ is changed into $f+dg$ - thus the set of $f$ \deleted{\unsure{p}}corresponding to different choices of $\handwritten{\phi}$ is exactly a \handwritten{3}-cohomology class
